claims.text: Menu is dominated by wheat-based items (ramen noodles, gyoza wrappers) and soy/oyster sauces, so cross-contamination with gluten is effectively unavoidable; no gluten-free protocol is documented.
As a Chinese restaurant, dishes use standard soy and brown sauces that typically contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

Kitchen centers on pork, egg, and seafood dishes (mapo tofu with pork, tenshinhan with egg, shark fin soup), so shared woks and broths make vegan-safe preparation unlikely; no vegan options documented.

name: おむすび 番旬 (Omusubi Banshun)

claims.text: The Nara tea-rice onigiri is offered in a soy-sauce version, and Japanese soy sauce normally contains wheat; takikomi-style rices such as the mackerel-and-ginger onigiri are also typically cooked with soy-sauce-based seasoning.

Many of the daily varieties contain fish, egg, or meat (salt-koji grilled salmon, mackerel rice, tamagoyaki, fried chicken), and the complimentary dine-in miso soup is not documented as vegan, so plant-based items are prepared in the same shop alongside animal products.
The salted Nara tea-rice onigiri (rice with roasted soybeans and hojicha) and the pickled-plum-and-shiso onigiri are plant-based in their core ingredients.

name: オステリア ユルリ (Osteria Yururi)

claims.text: Pasta and Italian dishes are central to the menu, so wheat is used heavily throughout the kitchen and cross-contact is likely; not suitable for celiacs.
The kitchen is built around charcoal-grilled pork, fish and meat plus house-made pancetta, so shared charcoal grill and surfaces make cross-contact with animal products likely for vegetable dishes.
Seasonal vegetables are sourced directly from local Nara farms and the chef grows reduced-pesticide rice used for the clay-pot rice, so plant ingredients are fresh and traceable.
An all-wheat bakery milling its own rye and using spelt and domestic wheat flour; flour is airborne throughout a small space, so heavy cross-contamination is unavoidable for anyone gluten-sensitive.

Butter, egg and dairy products are used widely (Yotsuba butter croissants, egg tarts, quiche), and breads are baked in shared ovens and handled in the same small workspace, so dairy/egg cross-contact with any 'plainer' loaf is likely.
Ingredient lists are kept simple and honest, with a focus on domestic wheat, organic self-milled rye, and a single named butter, which makes it easier to ask staff what is in a given loaf.
Beignets are a fried wheat-flour dough, with one variety made from rye and whole grain; no gluten-free option is documented and frying oil is shared.
Flavored beignets include cheese, white chocolate, caramel and nuts, indicating dairy and likely egg in the doughs; no vegan option is documented.
The chicory coffee is a caffeine-free, plant-based (roasted-root) drink.

name: Pleased To Meet Me（プリトミ） (Pleased To Meet Me)

claims.text: Falafel is deep-fried and typically served in a wheat pita; no information on dedicated fryers or flour use is documented, so gluten cross-contamination cannot be ruled out.
The kitchen also serves fish and dairy items (e.g., dairy-based ice cream floats), so a shared cooking surface and utensils are likely; vegans should specify their needs when ordering.
The falafel dish is explicitly described as containing no meat, and the venue openly lists vegan and vegetarian menu options.
The owner is friendly and approachable, which makes it easier to ask about ingredients in person.
The signature dish is wheat-panko-breaded deep-fried pork; the set rice is blended with barley, both gluten sources, so the meal is not gluten-free.
No allergen or soy-sauce ingredient information is documented; standard Japanese seasonings (typically wheat-containing soy sauce) should be assumed.
This is a pork specialty restaurant; even the vegetable soup contains imitation crab and no vegan main is offered.
The pork is fried in soybean oil at a low temperature, and meals come with a notably generous amount of vegetables and digestive teas.

name: キッシュ専門店　レ・カーセ (Quicheteria Le Case)

claims.text: The tart crust is made with whole-wheat (全粒粉) and rye (ライ麦粉) flour, so wheat/gluten is a core ingredient throughout the kitchen; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
Quiches are egg-, butter-, cheese- and cream-based and several use fish and shellfish (conger eel, scallop), so animal products are pervasive; no vegan options or separate vegan prep are documented.
Vegetables are organic and largely grown within Nara Prefecture, which the shop highlights as ingredients chosen so children can eat them safely.
